Adrenocortical carcinoma: Presence of large, pleomorphic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio in tumor cells.
Nuclear atypia with hyperchromatic and irregular nuclei.
Presence of necrosis within the tumor tissue.
Invasion into surrounding tissues, such as the capsule or blood vessels.
Presence of a fibrous capsule that may be breached by the tumor.
Trabecular, nested, or diffuse growth patterns.
Presence of clear cells, although less common.
Lipid-rich cytoplasm in some tumor cells, giving a vacuolated appearance.
Vascular invasion, which is a sign of aggressive behavior.
Presence of hemorrhage within the tumor.
Cytoplasmic granularity due to abundant mitochondria.
Bladder Urothelial Carcinoma: Thickened urothelium with more than 7 cell layers.
Presence of papillary structures with fibrovascular cores.
Nuclear atypia: enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with irregular contours.
Increased mitotic activity, including atypical mitoses.
Loss of polarity in the urothelial cells.
Presence of necrosis, often seen as comedo necrosis.
Invasion into the lamina propria or muscularis propria.
Prominent nucleoli within the urothelial cells.
Disorganized architecture compared to normal urothelium.

Brain Lower Grade Glioma: Increased cellularity: The tissue will show a higher density of cells compared to normal brain tissue.
Nuclear atypia: The nuclei of the tumor cells may appear irregular in shape and size, often larger than normal.
Mitotic figures: Presence of cells undergoing mitosis, indicating active cell division.
Microcystic changes: Small cyst-like spaces may be present within the tumor.
Fibrillary background: A fine, hair-like appearance in the background due to the presence of glial fibrils.
Perineuronal satellitosis: Tumor cells clustering around neurons.
Perivascular satellitosis: Tumor cells clustering around blood vessels.
Calcifications: Small, round, basophilic deposits may be present within the tumor.
Endothelial proliferation: Increased number of endothelial cells in blood vessels, sometimes forming glomeruloid structures.
Necrosis: Areas of cell death may be present, although less common in lower grade gliomas compared to higher grade tumors.
Infiltrative growth pattern: Tumor cells infiltrating into the surrounding normal brain tissue.
Oligodendroglial component: If present, cells may have a 'fried egg' appearance with clear cytoplasm and round nuclei.
Astrocytic component: If present, cells may have elongated, irregular nuclei and a fibrillary cytoplasm.
Breast invasive carcinoma: Irregularly shaped and infiltrative tumor cell clusters
Nuclear pleomorphism (variation in size and shape of nuclei)
Increased mitotic activity (presence of dividing cells)
Desmoplastic stroma (dense fibrous tissue surrounding tumor cells)
Loss of normal breast tissue architecture
Presence of necrosis (areas of cell death)
Lymphovascular invasion (tumor cells within blood vessels or lymphatics)
Presence of ductal or lobular structures depending on subtype
Presence of calcifications in some cases
Tumor cells may form glandular structures or sheets
Cervical squamous cell carcinoma and end: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma often shows nests or sheets of atypical squamous cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and intercellular bridges.
Keratinization is a key feature in squamous cell carcinoma, which may appear as keratin pearls or individual cell keratinization.
Nuclear atypia is prominent in squamous cell carcinoma, with enlarged, hyperchromatic, and pleomorphic nuclei.
Increased mitotic activity and abnormal mitotic figures are common in squamous cell carcinoma.
Endocervical adenocarcinoma typically presents with glandular structures or papillary formations lined by atypical columnar epithelial cells.
The cells in endocervical adenocarcinoma often have basally located nuclei and apical mucin, giving a pseudostratified appearance.
Nuclear atypia in adenocarcinoma includes enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli.
Endocervical adenocarcinoma may show intracytoplasmic mucin, which can be highlighted with special stains like mucicarmine or PAS.
Invasion into the stroma is a critical feature for both carcinomas, often accompanied by a desmoplastic stromal response.
Squamous cell carcinoma may show a more solid growth pattern, while adenocarcinoma tends to form glandular or papillary structures.
Inflammatory infiltrate, often lymphocytic, can be present in the stroma surrounding both types of carcinoma.
Necrosis and hemorrhage may be observed in both types of carcinoma, especially in poorly differentiated tumors.
Cholangiocarcinoma: Loss of normal bile duct architecture
Colon adenocarcinoma: Glandular formation: Look for irregular, distorted glandular structures that are atypical compared to normal colonic glands.
Nuclear atypia: Identify enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with irregular contours and prominent nucleoli.
Loss of polarity: Observe the disorganized arrangement of cells, losing the normal basal-apical orientation.
Increased mitotic activity: Note the presence of numerous mitotic figures, indicating rapid cell division.
Desmoplastic stroma: Look for dense, fibrous stroma surrounding the tumor glands, which is a reactive process to the tumor.
Necrosis: Identify areas of necrosis within the tumor, often seen as eosinophilic, amorphous debris.
Infiltrative growth pattern: Observe how the tumor invades into the surrounding tissue, breaking through the muscularis propria and beyond.
Mucin production: Some adenocarcinomas produce mucin, which can be seen as pools of extracellular mucin or intracellular mucin vacuoles.
Cribriform pattern: Look for back-to-back glandular structures with little intervening stroma, forming a cribriform pattern.
Signet ring cells: In some cases, identify cells with a large vacuole pushing the nucleus to the periphery, giving a signet ring appearance.
Esophageal carcinoma: Irregular nests or sheets of malignant squamous cells
Invasion into the submucosa or deeper layers
Loss of normal esophageal epithelium architecture
Glioblastoma multiforme: Hypercellularity: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is characterized by a high density of tumor cells, making the tissue appear densely packed.
Nuclear Atypia: The tumor cells often exhibit pleomorphic and hyperchromatic nuclei, which means the nuclei vary in size and shape and are darker than normal.
Mitotic Figures: Increased mitotic activity is common, with numerous mitotic figures visible, indicating rapid cell division.
Necrosis: Areas of necrosis are frequently present, often with pseudopalisading, where viable tumor cells line up around necrotic regions.
Vascular Proliferation: GBM often shows microvascular proliferation, with small, newly formed blood vessels that may appear glomeruloid.
Infiltrative Growth: The tumor cells infiltrate surrounding brain tissue, often blurring the boundary between tumor and normal tissue.
Endothelial Cell Hyperplasia: The blood vessels may show thickened walls due to increased endothelial cells.
Gemistocytic Cells: Some GBMs may contain gemistocytic astrocytes, which are large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
Microcystic Changes: Small cystic spaces may be present within the tumor tissue.
Perinecrotic Palisading: Tumor cells may line up in a palisading pattern around areas of necrosis.
Heterogeneity: The tumor may show a mix of different cell types and patterns, contributing to its 'multiforme' nature.
Increased N/C Ratio: The nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio is often increased, with large nuclei and scant cytoplasm.
Head and Neck squamous cell carcinoma: Keratin pearls: These are concentric layers of keratinized cells that appear as round, eosinophilic (pink) structures within the tumor.
Intercellular bridges: These are desmosomal connections between squamous cells, visible as thin lines or bridges between adjacent cells.
Pleomorphic nuclei: The nuclei of the cancer cells often vary in size and shape, indicating a high degree of pleomorphism.
Increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio: The nuclei of the cancer cells are larger relative to the amount of cytoplasm compared to normal cells.
Hyperchromatic nuclei: The nuclei appear darker than normal due to increased DNA content.
Mitotic figures: Increased number of cells undergoing mitosis, often abnormal in appearance, indicating rapid cell division.
Infiltrative growth pattern: The tumor cells invade surrounding tissues, often with irregular borders.
Loss of normal tissue architecture: The orderly arrangement of cells seen in normal tissue is disrupted.
Necrosis: Areas of cell death within the tumor, often appearing as regions of eosinophilic debris.
Desmoplastic stroma: A dense, fibrous stroma that may be present around the tumor cells.
Inflammatory infiltrate: Presence of lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells around the tumor.
Dyskeratosis: Abnormal keratinization occurring within individual cells or small clusters of cells.

Kidney renal clear cell carcinoma: Clear cytoplasm: The tumor cells typically have abundant clear cytoplasm due to the accumulation of glycogen and lipids, which are dissolved during tissue processing.
Round to polygonal cells: The cells are usually round to polygonal in shape.
Distinct cell borders: The cell borders are often distinct, making the cells appear well-defined.
Small, round nuclei: The nuclei are generally small and round, often located centrally within the cell.
Prominent nucleoli: The nucleoli within the nuclei are often prominent and can be seen clearly under the microscope.
Vascular network: There is often a rich network of small blood vessels (capillaries) within the tumor, giving it a highly vascular appearance.
Alveolar or nested growth pattern: The tumor cells are often arranged in nests or alveolar patterns, separated by thin-walled blood vessels.
Fibrous stroma: There may be a fibrous stroma that separates the nests of tumor cells.
Hemorrhage and necrosis: Areas of hemorrhage and necrosis can be present within the tumor.
Capsular invasion: The tumor may invade through the renal capsule into surrounding tissues.
Presence of psammoma bodies: Although less common, psammoma bodies (calcified structures) can sometimes be seen.
Kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma: Presence of foamy macrophages within the papillae
Psammoma bodies (calcified structures) may be present
Tumor cells with clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm

Presence of necrosis within the tumor
Thickened basement membranes around the papillae

Invasion into surrounding renal parenchyma or renal capsule
Liver hepatocellular carcinoma: Presence of bile production within tumor cells
Endothelial cell wrapping around tumor cell clusters
Fibrous capsule formation or lack thereof
Bile ductular reaction at the tumor periphery
Lung adenocarcinoma: Glandular formation: Look for irregular glandular structures, which are a hallmark of adenocarcinoma.
Cellular atypia: Identify cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli, indicating atypical cellular features.
Desmoplastic stroma: Observe the presence of fibrous or desmoplastic stroma surrounding the tumor cells.
Mucin production: Check for intracellular or extracellular mucin, which is often present in adenocarcinomas.
Papillary structures: Look for papillary formations, which can be a feature of some subtypes of lung adenocarcinoma.
Solid growth pattern: Identify areas where tumor cells form solid sheets or nests, lacking glandular differentiation.
Acinar pattern: Recognize small, round gland-like structures that resemble acini.
Lepidic growth pattern: Note tumor cells growing along pre-existing alveolar structures, preserving the lung architecture.
Pleomorphic cells: Identify variability in cell size and shape, which is common in malignant tumors.
Necrosis: Look for areas of necrosis within the tumor, which can be indicative of aggressive behavior.
Invasion: Observe for invasion into surrounding tissues, such as blood vessels or pleura.
Mitotic figures: Identify increased mitotic activity, which is a sign of rapid cell proliferation.
Lung squamous cell carcinoma: Keratinization: Look for keratin pearls or individual cell keratinization, which are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.
Intercellular Bridges: These are desmosomal connections between squamous cells, often visible in well-differentiated tumors.
Pleomorphic Cells: The presence of large, irregularly shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei.
High Nucleus-to-Cytoplasm Ratio: Squamous cell carcinoma cells often have a higher nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio compared to normal cells.
Mitotic Figures: Increased number of mitotic figures indicating high proliferative activity.
Necrosis: Areas of necrosis may be present, especially in poorly differentiated tumors.
Infiltrative Growth Pattern: The tumor may invade surrounding lung tissue, showing an irregular growth pattern.
Desmoplastic Stroma: The presence of a dense, fibrous stroma surrounding the tumor nests.
Inflammatory Infiltrate: Often, there is a lymphocytic infiltrate around the tumor.
Loss of Normal Lung Architecture: Disruption of the normal alveolar structure of the lung.

Mesothelioma: Presence of atypical mesothelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
Cells often form papillary structures or tubulopapillary patterns.

Ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma: Presence of slit-like spaces between papillae
Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma: Zellballen pattern: This is a characteristic nesting pattern of tumor cells surrounded by a fibrovascular stroma.
Polygonal cells: The tumor cells are typically polygonal with abundant granular cytoplasm.
Nuclear pleomorphism: There is often variation in nuclear size and shape, with some nuclei appearing hyperchromatic.
Salt and pepper chromatin: The nuclei often have a finely granular chromatin pattern, resembling salt and pepper.
Vascular stroma: A rich vascular network is often present, supporting the nests of tumor cells.
Cytoplasmic granularity: The cytoplasm of the tumor cells may appear granular due to the presence of catecholamine-containing granules.
Sustentacular cells: These are supporting cells that can be highlighted with immunohistochemical stains like S-100.
Capsular invasion: In some cases, the tumor may invade the capsule, which can be a sign of malignancy.
Necrosis: Areas of necrosis may be present, especially in larger tumors.
Mitoses: The presence of mitotic figures can vary, but increased mitotic activity may suggest a more aggressive tumor.
Fibrous septa: The nests of tumor cells are often separated by fibrous septa.
Cytoplasmic vacuolization: Some cells may show vacuolization of the cytoplasm.
Prostate adenocarcinoma: Glandular architecture: Look for small, crowded glands that are irregular in shape and size. These glands often lack the normal two-cell layer structure seen in benign prostate tissue.
Nuclear atypia: Observe for enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The nuclear size and shape may vary, and the chromatin may appear clumped or irregular.

Basal cell layer absence: In prostate adenocarcinoma, the basal cell layer is typically absent, which can be confirmed using immunohistochemical staining for basal cell markers like p63 or high molecular weight cytokeratin.
Infiltrative growth pattern: Note the invasion of cancerous glands into the surrounding stroma, which may disrupt the normal architecture of the prostate tissue.
Perineural invasion: Look for cancer cells surrounding or invading nerve fibers, which is a common feature in prostate adenocarcinoma.
Mitoses: Identify increased mitotic activity, which may be present in more aggressive forms of prostate adenocarcinoma.
Cribriform pattern: In some cases, a cribriform pattern may be observed, where glands form a sieve-like structure.
Necrosis: Although less common, central necrosis within glands can be a feature of high-grade prostate adenocarcinoma.
Amphophilic cytoplasm: The cytoplasm of the cancer cells may appear amphophilic, meaning it can stain with both acidic and basic dyes.
Gleason pattern: Recognize the Gleason grading patterns, which range from well-formed glands (pattern 3) to poorly formed or fused glands (pattern 4) and solid sheets of cells (pattern 5).
Rectum adenocarcinoma: Glandular formation: Look for irregular, distorted glandular structures that are atypical compared to normal rectal tissue.
Cellular atypia: Identify cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
Mitoses: Observe for increased mitotic figures, which indicate high cellular proliferation.
Desmoplastic stroma: Note the presence of dense, fibrous stroma surrounding the tumor glands.
Necrosis: Identify areas of necrosis within the tumor, which can appear as regions of cell death and debris.
Infiltrative growth pattern: Look for tumor cells invading the surrounding tissue, breaking through the normal architecture.
Loss of mucin production: Recognize reduced or absent mucin production in the tumor cells compared to normal goblet cells.
Cribriform pattern: Identify back-to-back glandular structures with little intervening stroma, forming a cribriform pattern.
Signet-ring cells: In some cases, look for signet-ring cells, which have a large vacuole pushing the nucleus to the periphery.
Lymphovascular invasion: Check for tumor cells within lymphatic or blood vessels, indicating potential for metastasis.
Perineural invasion: Look for tumor cells surrounding or invading nerves, which is a sign of aggressive behavior.

Uterine Corpus Endometrial Carcinoma: Glandular architecture: Look for irregular, crowded, and back-to-back glandular structures, which are often seen in endometrial carcinoma.

Mitotic figures: Observe for increased mitotic activity, which is a sign of rapid cell proliferation.
Loss of polarity: Note the disorganized arrangement of cells, which lose their normal orientation.
Necrosis: Identify areas of necrosis within the tumor, which can appear as regions of cell death and debris.
Stromal invasion: Look for tumor cells invading the surrounding stroma, which is a key feature of malignancy.
